q: Common causes of pneumonia in the first year of life include all EXCEPT:
The commonest cause of pneumonia in a 6-year-old child is:
e: Pneumococcus is the commonest bacterial cause at all ages after the newborn period.

q: A 9-year-old has fever, cough and crepitations; the X-ray shows consolidation with a pleural effusion. The most likely organism and treatment are:
o: Pneumococcus, treated with IV penicillin or ampicillin
e: Effusion and lobar consolidation point to bacteria; pneumococcus is the commonest cause of empyema.

q: Regarding mycoplasma pneumonia, which is CORRECT?
o: High fever and toxicity are usual
The chest X-ray often looks worse than the child
Lobar consolidation with large effusion is typical
Penicillins are the drugs of choice
e: Walking pneumonia: few signs, X-ray worse than the child; treat with a macrolide.

q: A 6-month-old is tachypnoeic if the respiratory rate is at least:
e: Fast breathing: ≥ 50/min at 2–11 months, ≥ 40/min at 1–5 years, ≥ 60/min under 2 months.

q: In lobar pneumonia, which sign is expected over the affected lobe?
o: Trachea shifted to the opposite side
e: Consolidation: dull note, bronchial breathing, increased vocal resonance; trachea central.

q: A 2-year-old has cough, RR 46/min and chest indrawing. He drinks well and has no danger signs. According to WHO 2024, the correct management is:
o: Oral amoxicillin for 5 days at home
Admission for IV ampicillin and gentamicin
e: Chest-indrawing pneumonia without danger signs: oral amoxicillin 40 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days at home.

q: A 14-month-old with cough has RR 52/min, cannot drink and is lethargic. The classification and treatment are:
o: Severe pneumonia: admit, oxygen, IV ampicillin + gentamicin
e: Any general danger sign makes it severe pneumonia.

q: A child on ampicillin and gentamicin for pneumonia still has fever after 48 hours, with stony dullness at the right base. The best next step is:
o: Chest X-ray and ultrasound, then pleural tap
e: Suspect effusion or empyema; confirm by imaging and tap the fluid.

q: Which pleural fluid finding defines an empyema?
e: Empyema: pus, organisms on Gram stain, pH < 7.2, low glucose, high LDH.

q: Pneumatoceles on the chest X-ray of an infant with skin boils suggest:
A child has three pneumonias in the right lower lobe in one year. The most likely cause is:
e: Same lobe each time → a local cause; different lobes → a general cause.
